name: Zoe Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the cards line for a regional bank, at their contact centre above the shopping arcade in town. People ring when their card's been blocked, when they've lost it, or when there's a payment they don't recognise. I check who they are, freeze the card, order a new one, and pass anything that looks like fraud to the fraud team upstairs. I like the fraud calls best, because it feels like you're actually protecting someone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how are you getting on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ten months. I'm still slow on the security checks, I always double-check, and my manager says that's fine for now but not forever. The bank gave us an AI helper that suggests what to say, and I use it when I'm stuck, maybe a few times a day. My boyfriend Jonas is an apprentice electrician, so neither of us earns much yet, and we've got about three weeks of money in the joint account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's kind of a relief, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad the hype calmed down, and that banks still need people people can trust. Online I'd probably not post anything, I'm not much for that. At work it'd be the usual chat over lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my job's fine in that one, banks always need someone on the phone for fraud. But I'm on low pay, my security checks are slow, and the bank closed two branches last year, so it's not like it's growing. And there aren't many other offices in town that hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and get my checks faster, using the AI helper more when I'm stuck. I'd apply for a junior spot on the fraud team when one comes up, because it pays a bit more. And Jonas and I would keep putting fifty a month aside each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A small worry in the background about money, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fraud team, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like it, and because it's harder to replace. Fraud is people lying to you, and you have to hear it in their voice. My friend Asha moved up last year and she says it's the best thing she's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Jonas's apprenticeship hits a slow patch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's my wage carrying us, and my wage isn't much. We'd cut back on eating out and visiting his family across the country. We'd manage for a month or two, but not longer.

I'd say banks still need **people you can trust** on the phone.

feel: **Okay** mostly, with a small **background worry** about money.

Save fifty a month each into the joint account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Yeah, that's me. Booking new cards too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible for the simple stuff, like ordering a new card, to go to the app. I'd also say banks need to be careful, because people panic about money and want a human. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the cards line shrinks a lot, because most of my calls are routine. The fraud team would last longer, but even they'd use AI to spot the odd payments. If I'm not on the fraud team in a year or two, I'm probably one of the people they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI helper on every call, not just when I'm stuck, so I get faster and learn how it works. I'd push hard for the fraud team, ask my manager straight what I need to do. And I'd look at an evening bookkeeping course, because small businesses always need someone to sort their books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Like I've been told I'm on the bubble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bookkeeping is thinking work too. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, it probably gets automated too. I think I picked it because it's what my mum did. Maybe I'd be better off learning something with Jonas, like helping on the electrical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas if the cuts came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we hold off on getting the car we've been looking at. He'd want to cover everything, he's like that, but his apprentice pay can't cover rent alone. We'd sit down with a notebook and do the sums.

I'd warn that people want **a human** when they panic about money.

fieldNote: She notices her **bookkeeping** idea is also exposed when gently challenged.

steps.text: Use the bank's AI helper on every call

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's really fast. I'd be twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to stay calm and see what the government does. I'd probably share the bank's own advice about what's changing. I wouldn't be one to make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the cards line and the fraud team both go, because it's all thinking work. The only bit of luck is Jonas, because electricians are hands-on and he'd have until robots come in 2031. So he'd probably keep earning for a few years while I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Jonas's boss if they take on a second apprentice, or even someone to do their paperwork and fetch parts. I'd stop all saving for the car and keep the money as a buffer. And I'd move us somewhere cheaper, maybe a room at his parents'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Mostly for me, a bit for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd become an electrician's apprentice at twenty-nine. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, but I'd rather be the oldest apprentice there than have nothing. I've helped Jonas with jobs at weekends and I didn't hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I really don't know. Maybe we'd both be out. I think by then everyone would be in the same boat, and the government would have to do something.

I'd share the bank's own **advice** rather than post opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like something you can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and people should plan, but not panic. At work I'd tell the younger ones to think about a trade. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd expect to be out of the bank by 2030 or so. But five years is enough to get an electrical qualification while I still have a wage. Then I'd have a few years doing hands-on work before the robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the evening electrical course, two nights a week, once I'd checked what Jonas's mates think of it. I'd keep using the AI helper at work to keep my numbers decent while I study. I'd save every bit of overtime into a training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I was doing something. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check with Jonas's mates first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'd know if the course is any good, or if it's a waste of money. I don't jump into things, so I want to hear from someone who's done the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, which is thirty a month, and going out on Saturdays. It'd be a boring couple of years. Jonas would probably moan, but he'd get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible. People should keep their jobs and learn new skills along the way. I'd probably say that over lunch and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the cards line still shrinks well before 2036, probably like the slow picture. So I'd still need to move, but I'd have time to see what works for others first. If the fraud team takes me, I might ride that a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the fraud team this year and use the AI tools properly. In a year or two I'd see whether people leaving for trades are doing well, and if so I'd start the electrical course. Jonas and I would start saving for a flat deposit, because ten years feels like enough time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a worry, but a slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still need to move. When would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I see two or three people from my floor lose their jobs, I'd know the change is real. Or when they do well somewhere else. I'm not going to be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I wait too long and the courses fill up with everyone else. Or that the rent eats everything and we never save. I know those are real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both my jobs on the floor would go at once and I'd have nothing ready. What would help is help paying for a trade course for people over twenty-five, and some kind of bridge payment while you're switching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this depends on your partner. I'm lucky my boyfriend is in a trade, because a lot of people on my floor don't have that.

headlineQuote: I'm lucky my boyfriend is in a trade, because a lot of people on my floor don't have that.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old** agent on a regional bank's **cards line**, ten months in and still slow on security checks.
She lives with her boyfriend, an **apprentice electrician**, with about three weeks of money.
She is **pragmatic**, uses the AI helper when stuck, and waits to see what works for others.
She hopes to reach the **fraud team**, then switches to an **electrical** course in the faster pictures.
Her partner's **hands-on trade** is the household's safety net in every AGI scenario.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because both roles on her floor go at once with **nothing ready**.
whatWouldHelp: Funding for **trade courses** for people over twenty-five.
